newsitem.title: RUSSIA: NATO and Russia agree terms for partnership pact.
newsitem.headline: NATO and Russia agree terms for partnership pact.

text.p: NATO and Russia agreed a deal on Wednesday intended to forge a peaceful new relationship after years of mistrust and sweep away Moscow's concerns over the expansion of the Western defence alliance.

The text of the deal was agreed at talks in Moscow between Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and NATO Secretary General Javier Solana after months of tough negotiations between the two former Cold War foes.

"The agreed text will be submitted for consideration to the NATO governments through the North Atlantic Council, and to (Russian) President (Boris) Yeltsin," Russia and NATO said in a joint statement.

A NATO source in Moscow said that once formal approval was obtained, the two sides were now "in readiness for signing on May 27". He was referring to the target date set by Yeltsin, who wants to sign the deal in Paris.
Details of the agreement were not immediately released and it was not clear if all differences had been fully resolved.

A breakthrough had been blocked until now by disagreements over whether the pact should include written guarantees that NATO will not station military structures and nuclear weapons on the territory of new member states.
The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation has been reluctant to give such guarantees in writing.
The agreement was concluded on the second day of talks between Solana and Primakov in a foreign ministry mansion in Moscow.
Yeltsin had spoken to Solana by telephone at around midday (0800 GMT) but it was not clear if he intervened in the talks before the pact was finalised.
Solana and Primakov had spent six hours on Tuesday trying to resolve differences over the document.
The talks had been shrouded by secrecy, but Solana and Primakov were due to speak to reporters at 2 p.m. (1000 GMT).
Yeltsin says he wants to sign an agreement with NATO on May 27 and said last week the deal was "98 percent" ready.

But, anxious to limit the criticism from his communist and nationalist foes, Yeltsin had also said he would not sign an unsatisfactory agreement and he told Primakov to take a tough line in the sixth round of Russia-NATO talks on the pact.
Yeltsin had also said repeatedly that Russia would not back NATO's plans to invite some eastern European countries to join the alliance at a summit in Madrid in July.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are expected to receive the first invitations to join NATO, though Romania and Slovenia also hope to be in the first wave.
Moscow regards enlargement as a security threat.
Yeltsin also wanted a deal to ensure a peaceful partnership with NATO and to keep relations with the West on track.
